_comment: Citations in docs/v2.0-roadmap.md that tools/check_roadmap_claims.py cannot
resolve and that are NOT stale: they name an artifact that is genuinely not
in this tree. Every entry carries the rule it suppresses, the exact claim key
the checker prints, and a written reason, in the shape the harness repo's
.github/ci/known-red.json uses.
An entry is NOT a way to silence a stale sentence. The checker reports any
entry that stops matching, so an allow-list line cannot outlive its reason.
A claim key is `<key>` for the path rule and `<symbol>@<path>` for the symbol
rule, printed verbatim by the checker. A citation that is stale and has to be
EDITED does not belong here; it belongs in tools/roadmap_claim_ratchet.json,
which is debt and is built to shrink.
Most of the path entries below name revl-HARNESS files. That repository is
this one's dogfood workload: the roadmap cites its components and scripts as
the place a gap was reproduced, and each sentence says revl-harness or the
harness in plain words. They became findings on 2026-09-24 (issue #1233) when
the path rule started judging bare backticked paths, and writing them down is
the point. Suppressing them by a prose cue instead was measured and refused:
a `revl-harness` window would have replaced 15 of these entries at the cost of
no longer judging 10 citations that resolve today and sit in the same
sentences.

entries.reason: Item 312 quotes `revl audit` OUTPUT from the out-of-tree lighthouse workload verbatim, to show the filename/line halves disagreeing. `src/services.rvl` is a path in THAT project, not in this repo, and rewriting the quote would destroy the evidence.

Item 421 F6 pins where `cordis::Value`'s hand-written `Debug` lives in UPSTREAM cordis-rs 0.6.2. The roadmap pins foreign repos this way throughout; this one carries its version in the path, so it stays resolvable by a reader without being a file here.

Item 57's gap is described against the revl-HARNESS dogfood workload, whose `tools/web_server.py` is a separate repository. The citation is to that project's host-side timer pump, which is the whole point of the finding: the behaviour cannot be expressed in-language and lives host-side, there.

Item 102's gap is that no lifecycle test can advance the clock, and the sentence names its counter-example in place: `tools/timer_demo.py` in revl-harness, the host driver that calls `Clock.advance` directly because nothing in-language can. It is that workload's file, and naming it IS the evidence.

Item 103 verifies slice-3 against the harness, and `wasm/canonical.rvl` is the revl-harness component holding the durable ledger's real pipe line format. The same sentence says milestone 31 in revl-harness, which is where the file lives.
Item 103's repro is a PASS-versus-REFUSED pair across the canonical ABI, and the PASS half is `tools/canonical_demo.py` in revl-harness, stated with the repository name in the same clause.

The REFUSED half of item 103's repro pair, in the same clause as `tools/canonical_demo.py` and in the same repository. It is the harness's own agent toolbox, whose `add_tool` reaches the `split` the wasm tier refuses.

Item 107 records where the harness hit the untyped-empty-list refusal while building its service-level canonical proof. `wasm/service.rvl` is that workload's component; the gap and the fix are in this repository's IR and emitters, which is what the item is about.
Item 449's repro is `mtier/agent.rvl` in revl-harness with the re-append restored, which the sentence says in those words. The clone bug it reproduces is in this repository's rust ownership pass.

Item 104 contrasts what the HARNESS can already launch end-to-end with what DSH's real plugins do at this repository's cordis importer. `tools/dsh_plugin_demo.py` is the harness-side launcher on the working side of that contrast.

Item 104 names its test corpus as the real DSH plugins and gives the path in the DSH checkout, in those words. DSH is a third project; the importer gaps the item lists are all in `src/revl/import_cordis.py` here.

Item 92's executable repro is the harness's async-migration branch, and `src/components/agent.rvl` with its `agent_loop` is the component on that branch. The coroutine leak it demonstrates is this repository's coloring gap.

Item 170's async timer gap is described against the revl-HARNESS dogfood workload, whose `tools/web_server.py` drives the scheduled automations HOST-SIDE. This is the path half of the `_start_automations@tools/web_server.py` entry above, made a claim of its own once the path rule began judging bare backticked citations.

Item 170's deliverable sentence says revl-harness grows the automation in `src/components/scheduler.rvl`. It names a file the harness will hold after the fix lands here, so it will never resolve in this tree.
The other half of item 170's deliverable, the revl-harness test file that is to prove a scheduled agent run fires on `Clock.advance`. Item 102 cites the same file for the same workload.

Item 348 records that revl-harness declares its whole composition in `src/manifest.rvl` and that its host bootstraps in two stages around it. The circularity is the finding; the manifest is the workload's file.

Item 361 says the repro lives in revl-harness `src/components/engine_model.rvl`, naming the repository in the same clause. The async match-block gap it reproduces is in this repository's parser and lowerer.

Item 367's hostage list is explicitly all measured in revl-harness lane H24, and the 268-line protocol-decode half it counts is that workload's MCP client. The item is about this repository's field-read totality; the file it counts the cost in is the harness's.

Item 373 quotes what the R-3 incident produced: a spawned coding agent inheriting ambient authority WROTE `src/plugins/bitcoin_price.rvl` into a live harness checkout. The path is the evidence of the escape, in someone else's tree, and it should never resolve here.

Item 484 spells it revl-harness `src/components/outbox.rvl` in the sentence itself, the H2 deliverable reduced to the crossing. The `deferred` modifier `revl audit` could not see is this repository's audit surface; the component carrying it is the harness's.

Finding F2's boundary argument uses `root/app.rvl` importing `../lib/x.rvl` as the example of an OPERATOR's own composition layout, the case the jail deliberately keeps compiling. It is an illustration inside one sentence, not a file anyone claims exists.

Finding F4 names a path INSIDE a deploy bundle, not inside this repository. `IR_DOCUMENT = "ir/ir.json"` in `src/revl/deploy.py` is the bundle-relative name, and deploy.py's own docstrings cite it the same way. It is produced, never tracked.

Item 519's `type/*` is a family of conformance CASE IDS, the nine signature cases in the generated matrix, and the sentence reads `type/*` declares a shape and computes nothing. It is a case namespace that happens to be spelled like a glob.

This is the roadmap item recording issue #1233 itself, which has to quote the harness-side and illustrative spellings that motivated the rule in order to explain it. The sentence names them as examples of what a judgement rule must tell apart.

Quoted in the same sentence as `src/components/*.rvl`, for the same reason: the item recording issue #1233 lists the harness-side spellings the widened path rule has to tell apart from a citation about this tree.
